query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-temperature HEAs, oxidation resistance is achieved because a key alloying element (e.g., Al or Cr) preferentially diffuses to the surface and forms a continuous, adherent, and protective oxide layer. The high mixing entropy promotes a uniform elemental distribution which, together with favorable kinetics for this element, leads to the selective formation of a protective oxide that reduces further oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar high-entropy alloy containing a known concentration of a critical oxidation‐resistant element (e.g., Al or Cr) uniformly distributed in the matrix.
generation.intervention: Fabricate a controlled compositional variation by preparing two HEA batches – one with the standard amount of the critical element and one intentionally reduced in that element. Alternatively, a tailored heat-treatment may be applied to enhance or retard the surface diffusion of this element.
generation.conditions: Expose both alloy variants to high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., 1000°C in air or oxygen-rich atmosphere) for a defined period (e.g., 100–200 hours) while monitoring weight gain and oxide scale morphology.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a surface-localized, dense oxide scale enriched in the critical element (Al or Cr), which acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the critical element diffuses faster to the alloy surface because of the high entropy, where it oxidizes to form a protective, low-diffusivity oxide. This oxide layer mitigates further oxygen ingress and slows oxidation on the bulk material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the variant with a reduced content of the critical element will develop a less continuous or thinner oxide scale, leading to higher oxidation rates (evidenced by greater weight gain and less protective scale morphology) under the same test conditions.
generation.baseline: The standard equimolar HEA containing the established level of the oxidation‐resistant element that reliably forms a protective oxide layer at high temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable under high-temperature oxidizing conditions (around 1000°C) and may not hold under lower temperature or non-oxidative environments. The effect is also contingent on the critical element concentration and the processing history ensuring homogeneous distribution.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of other elements and potential effects of microstructural factors such as grain boundaries or secondary phase formations are not fully quantified. Further studies are needed to determine the exact kinetics and elemental thresholds relevant to different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one with the standard concentration of the critical oxidation‐resistant element (e.g., Al or Cr) and one where this concentration has been significantly reduced. Subject both sets to oxidation at 1000°C in air for 100–200 hours. Characterize the weight gain over time, oxide scale continuity and composition by XPS, SEM/EDS, and phase analysis (XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both alloy sets exhibit comparable oxide scale continuity, composition, and oxidation rates, regardless of the different critical element concentrations, then the hypothesis that the selective oxidation of the critical element governs the formation of a protective oxide layer is falsified.
